title: Earth’s Rocks Have a Missing Layer Spanning Up to a Billion Years - Nautilus
gist: Flament and Dhungana (University of Wollongong), in new Nature research, explain the 150-year-old mystery of the Great Unconformity: mantle convection uplifted Laurentia, Baltica and North China from ~1 billion to 540 million years ago, coinciding with Snowball Earth ice sheets that scoured them, before they subsided and preserved younger sediment.

insights.claim: Geologists in the 1870s discovered on several continents a gap of hundreds of millions of years in the rock record, dubbed the Great Unconformity, which remained unexplained for 150 years.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Long-standing geological puzzles resolved by modeling show the payoff of compute-intensive geoscience.

insights.claim: At places like the Grand Canyon, flat sedimentary rock about 540 million years old or younger rests directly on crystalline basement up to two billion years old, meaning up to a quarter of Earth's history is missing.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Understanding basement exposure and erosion history matters for mineral and resource exploration models.
insights.quote: a considerable chunk (up to a quarter) of Earth’s history has simply vanished

insights.claim: Evidence of the Great Unconformity is found throughout North America, parts of northern China, and beneath younger rocks in northern Europe.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Geographic pattern provides a test case for the uplift explanation.

insights.claim: Competing explanations for the Great Unconformity included Snowball Earth ice-sheet erosion, continental reshuffling, mountain building, heat-induced internal movement, volcanism, and global sea-level change; testing was hard because the evidence is missing rock.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Illustrates inference from absence — a methodology challenge relevant to any data-gap problem.
insights.quote: Testing these hypotheses has been a challenge because the primary evidence consists of missing rock.

insights.claim: The sedimentary layers atop the Great Unconformity appear at the same time as the Cambrian explosion, which began around 540 million years ago.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Ties deep-Earth processes to the origin of complex life.
insights.locator: Important things happened in that time

insights.claim: Scientists have speculated that erosion of entire continents during the Great Unconformity may have altered seawater chemistry and allowed animal life to flourish.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Second-order link: geological erosion as a driver of ocean chemistry and biological change.
insights.quote: may have altered the chemical balance of seawater and allowed animal life to flourish

insights.claim: Earth's mantle is a 2,900-kilometre-thick layer of hot solid rock whose convection over tens to hundreds of millions of years can raise or lower continental surfaces by hundreds of metres.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Dynamic topography affects long-run sea level and basin formation — relevant to hydrocarbon and mineral basin models.
insights.quote: This huge, slow movement can raise or lower the surface by hundreds of metres.

insights.claim: The researchers used the Australian supercomputer Gadi to model how mantle movement affected continents over the past billion years.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: National HPC infrastructure enables frontier geoscience results.
insights.locator: We used the Australian supercomputer Gadi

insights.claim: Models consistently showed mantle convection lifted Laurentia, Baltica and North China from about a billion to 540 million years ago, then pulled them downward over the past 540 million years.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Uplift-then-subsidence history is the key mechanism; watch for follow-on validation in the field.
insights.quote: Our results consistently showed that mantle convection caused ancient continental blocks Laurentia

insights.claim: The uplift-then-subsidence sequence is ideal for both forming and preserving the Great Unconformity: uplift exposed and eroded the crystalline basement, and later sinking allowed new sediment to accumulate and be preserved.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Mechanistic explanation for where ancient basement rock is exposed.
insights.quote: This up-and-down movement is the ideal scenario for the formation and preservation of the Great Unconformity.
insights.locator: This up-and-down movement is the ideal

insights.claim: The modeled uplift coincided with Snowball Earth (720 to 635 million years ago), when enormous ice sheets scraped continental surfaces for tens of millions of years.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Combined mantle-plus-ice mechanism reconciles previously competing hypotheses.
insights.quote: the uplift predicted by our models coincided with the Snowball Earth period

insights.claim: Glaciers and ice sheets erode continents more efficiently than rivers, even on gentle slopes.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Glacial erosion efficiency matters for sediment-hosted resource formation.
insights.quote: Glaciers and ice sheets are more efficient than rivers at eroding continents, even on gentle slopes.

insights.claim: Australia and South America experienced only two cycles of uplift and subsidence since 900 million years ago, a scenario unfavorable to the Great Unconformity, and little evidence of it is seen there — supporting the model.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Negative control strengthens the explanation's credibility.

insights.claim: The authors conclude the Great Unconformity is a fingerprint of deep Earth processes that shaped the environment in which complex life first evolved.
insights.speaker: Nicolas Flament
insights.so_what: Frames deep-Earth dynamics as a driver of surface environment and biology.
insights.quote: the Great Unconformity is the fingerprint of deep Earth processes
